screens.title: Security Audits and Reviews
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will learn what a security audit is, why organizations perform audits, and how audits fit inside governance, risk, and compliance. A security audit is a formal, independent examination that checks whether controls are in place and operating as intended against defined criteria. Audits offer assurance to management, customers, and regulators that security aligns with risk appetite and legal obligations. You will also see the distinct roles of internal and external audits, how compliance and technical audits differ, and why a clear follow-up process turns findings into real improvements. For example, an audit might verify multi-factor authentication is enforced for remote access, then produce a finding and a recommendation to implement MFA where missing. A common misconception is that passing a compliance check equals being secure; in reality compliance is a snapshot and security requires continuous verification and remediation. By the end of this chapter you will understand audit phases, common evidence types, and how reports should separate findings from recommended actions. Consider how an audit in your organization could change a single control from being reactive to reliably managed.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Security Audits and Reviews
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Security Audits and Reviews

Audits confirm that controls match policy, regulatory criteria, and risk appetite. They are governance tools that produce evidence-based findings and specific recommendations for remediation.

In this lesson

You will learn audit types, the lifecycle from planning to follow-up, how to collect evidence, and how to interpret findings so they lead to improvement.

Why it matters

Audits provide documented assurance and a roadmap for fixing control gaps. They support regulators and build stakeholder trust.

Explore Key Topics
Audit Types

Internal, external, compliance, technical, and operational audits serve different assurance needs.

Audit Lifecycle

Planning, fieldwork, analysis, reporting, and follow-up form the audit lifecycle that closes the improvement loop.

Reporting

A clear report separates findings from recommendations and drives remediation tracking.

Concept Map
Controls
Policies, technical configs, processes
Evidence
Documents, logs, interviews
Findings
Observations and recommendations
Coming up

We'll step through audit types, evidence collection techniques, analysis and reporting, plus follow-up practices that ensure controls improve over time.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives describe the practical skills you will take away from this chapter. First, you will be able to define the purpose and scope of security audits within an organization's governance framework, so you can explain why audits are required and how they support risk management. Second, you will learn to differentiate between internal, external, compliance, technical, and operational audits, including when each is appropriate. Third, you will be able to explain the key phases of an audit — planning, fieldwork, analysis, reporting, and follow-up — and what evidence belongs in each phase. Finally, you will identify common audit standards and frameworks such as ISO 27001 and NIST CSF, and understand their relevance to audits. Each objective ties to practical tasks, like assembling an evidence packet, writing a finding, or preparing for a compliance assessment. Keep these outcomes in mind as we work through examples, since the goal is not only knowledge but the ability to perform basic audit activities that support governance and continuous improvement.

screens.title: What is a Security Audit?
screens.narratorSegment: A security audit is a structured, independent assessment that verifies whether an organization's information systems, policies, and operations comply with defined criteria such as laws, standards, or internal policy. Unlike a penetration test, which actively searches for exploitable vulnerabilities, an audit focuses on evidence that controls are present and operating effectively. For example, an audit might verify that access reviews are performed quarterly by examining review records and interviewing the control owner rather than attempting to bypass authentication. A common misconception is that an audit's goal is to find every vulnerability; instead, audits assess control design and operation relative to objectives. The practical significance is that audits provide assurance to management and external stakeholders and identify areas for improvement that governance teams must track. As you consider an audit, think about what success looks like: verifiable evidence that controls meet the stated criteria, clear documentation of exceptions, and actionable recommendations. To check your understanding, ask whether a given control is being verified for design, operation, or both. What is a Security Audit? means an audit verifies that controls meet established criteria and produces evidence-based findings rather than exploiting vulnerabilities.. In practical terms, a formal, independent examination to verify controls against criteria. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › What is a Security Audit?
Core Concept

Security Audit

A formal, independent examination that confirms controls meet specific criteria and operate effectively.

Key points
  • Audits compare evidence to criteria: policy, regulation, or standard.
  • Purpose is assurance and improvement, not active exploitation.
  • Findings are classified as observations, control deficiencies, or non-compliance.
Example
Verify quarterly access reviews by reviewing review logs and approvals rather than attempting to circumvent controls.
Key Takeaway

Audits provide evidence-based assurance; they document what works and what needs fixing.

Definition panel
Evidence types
  • Document review (policies, diagrams)
  • Interviews with control owners
  • Observation of processes
  • Technical configuration checks
Common mistake

Treating compliance as equivalent to security. Compliance is a point-in-time check; security requires ongoing assurance and improvement.

Check your understanding

How would you prove that a control is operating effectively for the last six months? Identify two evidence sources you would collect.

screens.title: Types of Security Audits
screens.narratorSegment: Security audits come in several flavors and each serves a different assurance purpose. Internal audits are performed by staff within the organization who are independent of operations; their role is proactive improvement and preparation for external reviews. External audits are done by independent third parties and are often required for regulatory or contractual reasons; they provide an unbiased opinion for external stakeholders. Compliance audits focus explicitly on adherence to laws or standards such as PCI DSS or GDPR, verifying required controls and evidence. Technical audits zoom into configurations and system settings to ensure technical controls are implemented according to policy; they verify patch levels, firewall rules, and access controls. Operational audits examine the effectiveness of processes like incident response or change management. A common misconception is to treat technical testing as a complete audit; while technical checks are important, they do not replace governance-focused evidence like documented processes and management sign-offs. For practical use, map the audit type to the audience and objective: internal for management improvement, external for stakeholder assurance, compliance for legal requirements, technical for configuration validation, and operational for process effectiveness. Which audit type would best address your most critical risk right now?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Types of Security Audits
Comparison

Audit types at a glance

Match each audit type to its focus, typical evidence, and audience.

Internal Audit
Objective: management assurance and improvement. Evidence: process records, internal controls, self-assessments.
External Audit
Objective: external assurance. Evidence: formal controls, independent testing, compliance artifacts.
Compliance Audit
Objective: legal or standard adherence. Evidence: mapped controls, attestations, proof of process.
Technical Audit
Objective: configuration validation. Evidence: system settings, patch records, scans.
Operational Audit
Objective: process effectiveness. Evidence: incident records, change logs, access reviews.
Deeper look
Practical example

For PCI DSS, a compliance audit will require cardholder data flow diagrams, configuration evidence for segmentation, and formal attestation.

Misconception

Assuming a successful technical scan proves compliance. Scans help, but compliance needs documented controls and processes too.

Key Takeaway

Pick audit type by the question you need answered: manage risk, prove compliance, validate configuration, or improve processes.

screens.title: Audit Lifecycle: Planning and Scoping
screens.narratorSegment: Planning and scoping are the foundation of an effective audit. During planning you define what the audit will cover, the audit objectives, the criteria against which you will assess controls, and the resources required. Clear scoping avoids scope creep and ensures auditors collect relevant evidence. For example, if the objective is to verify least privilege for a financial application, scope should name the application, user groups, timeframes, and which access logs or approval records will be examined. A practical planning checklist includes: identify stakeholders, select audit criteria (policy, regulation, or standard), set a timeline, and define deliverables. A common mistake is leaving criteria implicit; auditors need explicit standards to evaluate evidence consistently. Good scoping also assigns responsibility for evidence collection and lists the types of evidence expected. In short, planning turns a vague assurance question into specific, testable steps. Ask yourself: if you could collect only three pieces of evidence for this audit, which would they be and why? In practical terms, set objectives, scope, criteria, and resources to avoid scope creep. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Audit Lifecycle: Planning
Process Flow

Planning & Scoping

Define objectives, scope, criteria, stakeholders, and deliverables so the audit is measurable and focused.

Step 1
Define objectives
Step 2
Set scope
Step 3
Choose criteria
Step 4
Assign resources
Example scope

Objective: verify least privilege for the financial application. Scope: production application servers, admin accounts, approval logs from the last 12 months.

Planning checklist
  • Identify stakeholders and evidence owners.
  • Document criteria and acceptance thresholds.
  • Define timeline and deliverables.
  • List expected evidence sources and formats.
Common mistake

Leaving criteria vague. Without explicit criteria, evidence evaluation becomes subjective and inconsistent.

Key Takeaway

Clear, measurable scope and criteria are the controls that make an audit reliable and repeatable.

screens.title: Fieldwork and Evidence Collection
screens.narratorSegment: Fieldwork is where auditors gather the evidence that supports findings. Evidence collection methods include document review, interviews with responsible personnel, direct observation of processes, and technical testing or sampling. Document review could include policies, network diagrams, access logs, and past audit reports. Interviews help verify ownership and process understanding. Observation confirms that processes actually happen as described. Technical sampling might check patch status or firewall rules on a subset of systems. Use multiple evidence types to triangulate conclusions; a document saying a process exists is stronger when combined with interview confirmation and observed practice. A common pitfall is relying on a single evidence type, such as only reading policies without corroboration. During fieldwork, maintain clear evidence mapping back to criteria, record timestamps and sources, and note any limitations in evidence. For practice, when auditing an access review, collect the access policy, most recent review sign-offs, access lists, and logs of account changes to demonstrate the process works end-to-end. Fieldwork and Evidence Collection means combine document review, interviews, observation, and technical sampling to build credible, traceable evidence for findings.. In practical terms, collect documents, interviews, observations, and technical samples. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Fieldwork and Evidence Collection
Fieldwork

Methods of evidence collection

Use a mix of document review, interviews, observation, and technical sampling to substantiate audit claims.

Document Review
Policies, diagrams, previous reports, and logs.
Interviews
Confirm roles, responsibilities, and practice from people who operate controls.
Observation
Watch processes occur, such as backups or access reviews, to confirm execution.
Technical Sampling
Check configurations, patch levels, and logs on representative systems.
Practical example

For an access review: collect the access policy, the most recent review sign-offs, current access lists, and logs of recent account changes or approvals.

Common mistake

Relying solely on policy documents without confirming that procedures are followed operationally.

Key Takeaway

Triangulate evidence from multiple sources to support reliable findings and reduce ambiguity for remediation owners.

screens.title: Analysis, Findings, and Recommendations
screens.narratorSegment: After evidence is collected, auditors analyze it against the predefined criteria to identify findings. Findings are observations about control operation and typically fall into categories such as observations, control deficiencies, or non-compliance. Effective analysis determines root cause and potential business impact so that recommendations are prioritized. A clear audit report separates the finding — what was observed and why it fails the criteria — from the recommendation — what should be done to remediate. For example, a finding might state that multi-factor authentication was not enforced for remote administrative access, citing configuration screenshots and access logs as evidence. The recommendation would then specify a corrective action such as enabling MFA for those accounts and a suggested timeline. A common error is to write vague recommendations like "improve controls" that lack specific action and owners. Good recommendations include the action, responsible owner, and timeframe so follow-up can be tracked. Conclude each finding with a measurable acceptance criterion, and ask: how will we know when this finding is closed? Analysis, Findings, and Recommendations means separate findings (evidence-based observations) from recommendations (specific, assigned corrective actions) and include acceptance criteria.. In practical terms, classify findings and write actionable recommendations that close gaps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Analysis, Findings, and Recommendations
Analysis & Evaluation

From evidence to findings

Classify observations, identify root causes, and assess impact to craft prioritized, actionable recommendations.

Finding
What was observed and which criteria it fails.
Root Cause
Why the control failed (process, people, or technology).
Recommendation
Specific corrective action, owner, and timeline.
Example finding and recommendation
Finding: Remote admin accounts lacked multi-factor authentication; evidence: config screens and access logs. Recommendation: Enable MFA on all remote admin accounts within 30 days; owner: IT security.
Common mistake

Writing vague recommendations without a responsible owner or measurable acceptance criteria.

Key Takeaway

Findings must be evidence-based and recommendations must be specific, assigned, and measurable to enable effective follow-up.

Check your understanding

When writing a recommendation, include the action, the owner, and the timeframe — how would you phrase that for a weak password policy?

screens.title: Audit Criteria: ISO/IEC 27001 and NIST CSF
screens.narratorSegment: Audit criteria are the standards, policies, and regulations auditors use to evaluate evidence. ISO/IEC 27001 is an international standard for an Information Security Management System; an ISO 27001 audit checks that an organization has established, implemented, maintained, and continually improved its ISMS. Auditors verify documentation, risk assessments, control implementation, and evidence of continual improvement. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is a voluntary set of standards, guidelines, and best practices organized around Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. Organizations can map controls and assessments to the CSF functions as audit criteria even though CSF is not a certification standard in the same way as ISO 27001. Other domain-specific criteria include PCI DSS for cardholder data or HIPAA for protected health information. A common misconception is to assume the framework alone guarantees security; instead, frameworks provide criteria and structure for audits but effective security requires accurate implementation and continuous checks. When scoping an audit, select the framework that best matches the organization’s objectives and the stakeholders who will use the report. In practical terms, how common frameworks provide audit criteria and structure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Audit Criteria: ISO/IEC 27001 and NIST CSF
Comparison

ISO 27001 vs NIST CSF

ISO 27001 supports certification of an ISMS; NIST CSF provides voluntary functions for risk management and control mapping.

ISO/IEC 27001
Audit verifies documented ISMS, risk assessment, control implementation, and continual improvement evidence.
NIST CSF
Framework maps controls to Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover; useful as audit criteria but not a certification in all cases.
Practical use

Select criteria that match stakeholders: ISO for certification and external assurance, CSF for internal risk alignment and control mapping.

Example mapping

Map a control such as access control to NIST CSF Protect function and to ISO 27001 annex controls to create audit test steps.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Audit Reporting
Reporting

Structure and tone

Executive summary, scope, methodology, findings with evidence, recommendations, and follow-up plan.

Executive Summary
Highlight major risks and prioritized actions for leadership.
Appendices
Store raw evidence and technical details that support findings.
Example finding text
Finding: Lack of multi-factor authentication for remote admin access. Evidence: access logs and configuration screenshots. Impact: increased risk of unauthorized access. Recommendation: Implement MFA for all remote administrative accounts within 30 days; owner: IT security; acceptance: MFA verified on 100% of targeted accounts.
Key Takeaway

Make findings evidence-first and recommendations specific, measurable, and assigned so action is straightforward.

screens.title: Follow-up, Remediation, and Continuous Improvement
screens.narratorSegment: Follow-up is the phase that turns audit recommendations into improved security. After reporting, remediation owners implement corrective actions and auditors or designated reviewers verify that those actions are completed and operating as intended. Effective follow-up includes tracking each recommendation with an owner, target date, and acceptance criteria. Auditors may perform a follow-up review or re-audit to validate the remediation. Continuous improvement occurs when organizations use audit trends to strengthen controls and adjust policies, not merely to close tickets. For example, if several audits show weak access review practices, remediation might include process redesign, automation of reviews, and updated training. A frequent mistake is treating follow-up as a single closure tick; instead, verify operation and measure whether the control reduces risk. To make follow-up effective, include measurable acceptance criteria in recommendations and set periodic review milestones until the control demonstrates sustained operation. Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Follow-up, Remediation, and Continuous Improvement
Follow-up

Track and verify remediation

Assign owners, set dates, and define acceptance criteria so recommendations become sustained controls.

Track
Log owner, status, and target completion date.
Verify
Re-check evidence and operation after remediation.
Improve
Use trends to update controls and processes.
Example

If access reviews repeatedly miss privileged accounts, remediation could include automated review tooling, role redesign, and quarterly audit verification for two cycles.

Pro tip

Define measurable acceptance criteria at the time of recommendation to avoid ambiguity during follow-up.

Key Takeaway

Follow-up is the mechanism that makes audits useful; track, verify, and use lessons learned to improve controls over time.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will learn what a security audit is, why organizations perform audits, and how audits fit inside governance, risk, and compliance. A security audit is a formal, independent examination that checks whether controls are in place and operating as intended against defined criteria. Audits offer assurance to management, customers, and regulators that security aligns with risk appetite and legal obligations. You will also see the distinct roles of internal and external audits, how compliance and technical audits differ, and why a clear follow-up process turns findings into real improvements. For example, an audit might verify multi-factor authentication is enforced for remote access, then produce a finding and a recommendation to implement MFA where missing. A common misconception is that passing a compliance check equals being secure; in reality compliance is a snapshot and security requires continuous verification and remediation. By the end of this chapter you will understand audit phases, common evidence types, and how reports should separate findings from recommended actions. Consider how an audit in your organization could change a single control from being reactive to reliably managed.

These learning objectives describe the practical skills you will take away from this chapter. First, you will be able to define the purpose and scope of security audits within an organization's governance framework, so you can explain why audits are required and how they support risk management. Second, you will learn to differentiate between internal, external, compliance, technical, and operational audits, including when each is appropriate. Third, you will be able to explain the key phases of an audit — planning, fieldwork, analysis, reporting, and follow-up — and what evidence belongs in each phase. Finally, you will identify common audit standards and frameworks such as ISO 27001 and NIST CSF, and understand their relevance to audits. Each objective ties to practical tasks, like assembling an evidence packet, writing a finding, or preparing for a compliance assessment. Keep these outcomes in mind as we work through examples, since the goal is not only knowledge but the ability to perform basic audit activities that support governance and continuous improvement.

These additional objectives focus on the practical actions auditors perform and the communication that makes audits useful. You will learn to plan fieldwork and choose evidence collection techniques such as document review, interviews, observation, and technical sampling. You will develop analysis skills to classify findings, determine root causes, and assess impact so recommendations are focused and actionable. You will also practice writing clear audit reports that distinguish findings from recommendations and include evidence that supports each claim. Finally, you will learn follow-up and remediation tracking so audit recommendations become completed improvements, not checklist items. For example, you will prepare a short finding that states the evidence, the control deficiency, and a prioritized recommendation. A common error is mixing findings and recommendations in the same sentence; separating them improves clarity for remediation owners. These skills bridge the gap between verification and continuous security improvement.

A security audit is a structured, independent assessment that verifies whether an organization's information systems, policies, and operations comply with defined criteria such as laws, standards, or internal policy. Unlike a penetration test, which actively searches for exploitable vulnerabilities, an audit focuses on evidence that controls are present and operating effectively. For example, an audit might verify that access reviews are performed quarterly by examining review records and interviewing the control owner rather than attempting to bypass authentication. A common misconception is that an audit's goal is to find every vulnerability; instead, audits assess control design and operation relative to objectives. The practical significance is that audits provide assurance to management and external stakeholders and identify areas for improvement that governance teams must track. As you consider an audit, think about what success looks like: verifiable evidence that controls meet the stated criteria, clear documentation of exceptions, and actionable recommendations. To check your understanding, ask whether a given control is being verified for design, operation, or both. What is a Security Audit? means an audit verifies that controls meet established criteria and produces evidence-based findings rather than exploiting vulnerabilities.. In practical terms, a formal, independent examination to verify controls against criteria. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Security audits come in several flavors and each serves a different assurance purpose. Internal audits are performed by staff within the organization who are independent of operations; their role is proactive improvement and preparation for external reviews. External audits are done by independent third parties and are often required for regulatory or contractual reasons; they provide an unbiased opinion for external stakeholders. Compliance audits focus explicitly on adherence to laws or standards such as PCI DSS or GDPR, verifying required controls and evidence. Technical audits zoom into configurations and system settings to ensure technical controls are implemented according to policy; they verify patch levels, firewall rules, and access controls. Operational audits examine the effectiveness of processes like incident response or change management. A common misconception is to treat technical testing as a complete audit; while technical checks are important, they do not replace governance-focused evidence like documented processes and management sign-offs. For practical use, map the audit type to the audience and objective: internal for management improvement, external for stakeholder assurance, compliance for legal requirements, technical for configuration validation, and operational for process effectiveness. Which audit type would best address your most critical risk right now?

Planning and scoping are the foundation of an effective audit. During planning you define what the audit will cover, the audit objectives, the criteria against which you will assess controls, and the resources required. Clear scoping avoids scope creep and ensures auditors collect relevant evidence. For example, if the objective is to verify least privilege for a financial application, scope should name the application, user groups, timeframes, and which access logs or approval records will be examined. A practical planning checklist includes: identify stakeholders, select audit criteria (policy, regulation, or standard), set a timeline, and define deliverables. A common mistake is leaving criteria implicit; auditors need explicit standards to evaluate evidence consistently. Good scoping also assigns responsibility for evidence collection and lists the types of evidence expected. In short, planning turns a vague assurance question into specific, testable steps. Ask yourself: if you could collect only three pieces of evidence for this audit, which would they be and why? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Fieldwork is where auditors gather the evidence that supports findings. Evidence collection methods include document review, interviews with responsible personnel, direct observation of processes, and technical testing or sampling. Document review could include policies, network diagrams, access logs, and past audit reports. Interviews help verify ownership and process understanding. Observation confirms that processes actually happen as described. Technical sampling might check patch status or firewall rules on a subset of systems. Use multiple evidence types to triangulate conclusions; a document saying a process exists is stronger when combined with interview confirmation and observed practice. A common pitfall is relying on a single evidence type, such as only reading policies without corroboration. During fieldwork, maintain clear evidence mapping back to criteria, record timestamps and sources, and note any limitations in evidence. For practice, when auditing an access review, collect the access policy, most recent review sign-offs, access lists, and logs of account changes to demonstrate the process works end-to-end. After evidence is collected, auditors analyze it against the predefined criteria to identify findings. Findings are observations about control operation and typically fall into categories such as observations, control deficiencies, or non-compliance. Effective analysis determines root cause and potential business impact so that recommendations are prioritized. A clear audit report separates the finding — what was observed and why it fails the criteria — from the recommendation — what should be done to remediate. For example, a finding might state that multi-factor authentication was not enforced for remote administrative access, citing configuration screenshots and access logs as evidence. The recommendation would then specify a corrective action such as enabling MFA for those accounts and a suggested timeline. Good recommendations include the action, responsible owner, and timeframe so follow-up can be tracked. Conclude each finding with a measurable acceptance criterion, and ask: how will we know when this finding is closed? Audit criteria are the standards, policies, and regulations auditors use to evaluate evidence. ISO/IEC 27001 is an international standard for an Information Security Management System; an ISO 27001 audit checks that an organization has established, implemented, maintained, and continually improved its ISMS. Auditors verify documentation, risk assessments, control implementation, and evidence of continual improvement. Other domain-specific criteria include PCI DSS for cardholder data or HIPAA for protected health information. A common misconception is to assume the framework alone guarantees security; instead, frameworks provide criteria and structure for audits but effective security requires accurate implementation and continuous checks. When scoping an audit, select the framework that best matches the organization’s objectives and the stakeholders who will use the report.
